findings.detail: runReadOnly returns network_isolation_unavailable for the entire remaining command list when the first command without a network grant encounters no isolation prefix. runGrade marks each command individually (line 627-628: per-command result, not a function-level return). In a multi-command plan where cmd[0] has no grant and cmd[1] has network:true, runReadOnly never runs cmd[1] and returns early; runGrade would run cmd[1] as granted. The AT-LF-22 oracle test uses single-command scenarios that don't expose this. The behavior satisfies AT-LF-22's letter (the connection doesn't succeed), but the asymmetry between the two runners means a legitimate granted command after an ungrantable one is silently skipped in the read-only path.

The AT-LF-20 oracle test reuses the same JS approval object for both the first and second executePlan calls. The first call sets approval.used = true (line 486 of lint-format.js), so the second call is blocked by the in-memory flag rather than the durable on-disk record. This is the weaker version of the one-use guarantee. The cross-object, cross-process case (the guarantee that actually matters) is proven by AT-PROC-1a in guarantee-coverage.test.js, which is non-frozen. The oracle test exercises a valid subset but would pass even if the durable filesystem mechanism were removed, as long as the JS object flag remained.

When network state is 'undeclared' (neither 'none' nor 'required'), runConfiguredArgv runs the command without any isolation prefix and emits a console.warn diagnostic (line ~196). The AD-39 spec says 'undeclared network state remains a visibly reported compatibility state.' This is implemented as expected, but the diagnostic goes to stderr rather than being returned as a structured field the caller can route into a named non-passing result. The oracle test AT-CAP-3 verifies the undeclared state is returned as a diagnostic field, which AT-PROC-1u also verifies. The behavior is compliant with the spec but the console.warn output is a silent stderr emission that callers could miss.
